title: Tokens: how a model reads
subtitle: Byte-pair encoding, merge by merge, with TinyGPT's real 256-token vocab

segments.text: Models can't read letters. They only eat numbers. So how does a word like Wednesday get in?
segments.scene: The word 'wednesday' in big letters above a box labelled 'the model — only eats numbers', with an arrow and '[ ?, ?, ? ]' between them.

objects.label: TinyGPT only accepts integer token ids (0–255)

segments.text: The simplest trick is one number per character. Our model starts with 35 base symbols. 26 letters, space, newline, six punctuation marks, and an unknown token.
segments.scene: A grid of the 35 base tokens with their ids: <unk> (0), newline (1), space (2), a–z (3–28), and . , ? ! : ' (29–34).

segments.text: But then Wednesday costs ten tokens, and the model has to re-spell every common word from scratch. Slow, and wasteful.
segments.scene: ' wednesday' (with its leading space, shown as ␣) split into 10 single-character chips with ids 2, 25, 7, 6, 16, 7, 21, 6, 3, 27. Flash: '10 tokens for one word?!'

segments.text: Byte-pair encoding fixes this. Scan the training text and count every pair of neighbors. The winner is space t, 13,558 times. Merge it into a brand new token, and repeat.
segments.scene: A corpus snippet at the top; bars of the most frequent adjacent pairs in the first 400k characters: '␣+t' 13,558, 'h+e' 11,868, '␣+a' 10,413, 't+h' 10,372. The winner becomes new token #35 '␣t'.

objects.label: a slice of the synthetic tiny-world training corpus

segments.text: The first four merges already build 'the', with its space. Each merge is a rule, and the rules are kept in the order they were learned.
segments.scene: Left: the first four merge rules (␣+t→␣t id 35, h+e→he id 36, ␣+a→␣a id 37, ␣t+he→␣the id 38). Right: '␣the' fusing from 4 characters into one token, id 38.

objects.label: token " the" = id 38, built by rules 1, 2 and 4

segments.text: Do that 221 times, and you get 35 plus 221. A vocabulary of exactly 256 tokens.
segments.scene: Big equation: 35 base symbols + 221 merges = 256 vocab size.

segments.text: To encode new text, start from characters and replay the merges in the order they were learned. Space w goes first, then a y, then e d.
segments.scene: ' wednesday' as 10 character chips; below, a panel shows the merge being applied. Merges fire in learned order: ␣+w → ␣w (rank 9), a+y → ay (rank 10), e+d → ed (rank 13).

segments.text: Then e s. Then d plus ay makes day, and es plus day makes esday. Ten characters, four tokens.
segments.scene: Remaining merges: e+s → es, d+ay → day, es+day → esday. Final result: ␣w (43) · ed (47) · n (16) · esday (202) — 4 tokens.

segments.text: Notice the splits ignore grammar. 'esday' exists because Tuesday and Wednesday share it. Jumping becomes space, j, um, p, ing. The model never sees inside a token.
segments.scene: Examples: ' tuesday' → ␣t · u · esday (shares 'esday', id 202, with wednesday); ' jumping' → ␣ · j · um · p · ing.

segments.text: Frequent words get a token all to themselves. Space red is just ID 157, one single chunk.
segments.scene: ' red' → a single token, id 157.

segments.text: Our vocab has 256 entries. GPT-2 had 50,257. Newer models go past 100 thousand. Same algorithm, bigger table.
segments.scene: Vocab-size bars to scale: TinyGPT 256 (a sliver), GPT-2 50,257, newer LLMs 100k+. Flash: 'same algorithm, bigger table'.

segments.text: A bigger vocab means shorter sequences, but a bigger embedding table. It's a knob you'll get to turn when you build your own.
segments.scene: Trade-off: bigger vocab → fewer tokens per sentence but a bigger embedding table (TinyGPT 256×64 = 16,384 numbers; GPT-2 50,257×768 = 38.6 million).

objects.label: trade-off: bigger vocab = shorter sequences but more embedding parameters

title: Embeddings: words as directions
subtitle: The lookup table that turns token ids into 64 numbers, and the meaning hiding in them

segments.text: To this model, the word red is token 157. Just a row number. So how does a number come to mean anything?
segments.scene: A big token chip '␣red' with its id 157 underneath and the question 'what does 157 mean?'.

objects.label: token " red" has id 157 in the 256-token vocabulary

segments.text: The very first step is a lookup table. 256 rows, one per token, 64 numbers in each row. Token 157 just grabs row 157. That row is its embedding.
segments.scene: The real 256×64 embedding table as a heatmap (orange positive, blue negative). Row 157 is outlined and slides out as a strip of 64 cells; its first values are -0.17, -0.14, -0.18, +0.07 … -0.19.

embedding of " red" (row 157): 64 numbers from -0.28 to +0.28, length 1.18

segments.text: All 16,384 of these numbers started as random noise. Training nudged them, until tokens used the same way got similar rows.
segments.scene: Same view; caption: 'started random → shaped by training'. The table holds 16,384 of the model's 170,560 parameters.

segments.text: No single number means red. What matters is the direction the whole row points. We compare directions with cosine similarity: one means same way, zero means unrelated.
segments.scene: Toy 2-D picture: arrows for ' red' and ' purple' point almost the same way, ' tom' points elsewhere. Text: cosine similarity = how aligned two arrows are (+1 same way, 0 unrelated, −1 opposite).

segments.text: Sixty-four numbers is tiny. GPT-3's largest version uses 12,288 per token, 192 times the room. More directions means more distinctions it can keep apart at once.

title: Attention, visually
subtitle: Queries, keys, values, softmax — and a real head that copies colors

segments.text: How does the word 'the' know to look back at 'red'? Attention. Let's build it from three arrows.
segments.scene: The prompt start 'mia has a red ball' … 'tom has the' with a yellow curved arrow from the last ' the' back to ' red' and a question mark.

segments.text: Every token turns its vector into three new ones. A query that asks, what am I looking for. A key that says, here's what I've got. And a value, the info it hands over if it gets picked.
segments.scene: The token ' the' spawns three arrows: query (blue) 'what am I looking for?', key (teal) 'what do I contain?', value (orange) 'what do I hand over if picked?' — each = x · a learned matrix.

objects.label: token " the" — its vector x feeds three learned matrices
query vector: what this token is looking for
key vector: what this token offers to be found by
value vector: the information it passes on

segments.text: To score a match, take the dot product of a query with each earlier key. Pointing the same way scores high. At right angles, zero. Opposite, negative.
segments.scene: Toy 2-D plane: a blue query arrow and a teal key arrow sweeping around it; a live readout of q · k goes high when aligned, 0 at right angles, negative when opposite.

segments.text: Do it for every earlier token, and you get one score each. Red's key lines up with the query, so it scores highest.
segments.scene: Three toy keys for ' red', ' mia', ' ball' drawn in the plane; a table of dot products: ' red' +4.8, ' mia' +0.2, ' ball' −0.8.

segments.text: Divide by the square root of the vector size, then softmax. Every score becomes a positive weight, and the weights add up to one.
segments.scene: Score bars (q·k/√2: ' red' +3.39, ' mia' +0.14, ' ball' −0.57) morph into softmax weight bars: ' red' 94.5%, ' mia' 3.7%, ' ball' 1.8%.

segments.text: The output is the weighted sum of the values. So it's mostly the value of whatever matched best.
segments.scene: Left: the three weights shrink to the side. Right: toy value vectors (orange) for ' red', ' mia', ' ball'; scaled by their weights and added tip to tail, they give the yellow output arrow — almost exactly red's value.

objects.label: toy value vectors v for ' red', ' mia', ' ball'

segments.text: One rule. No peeking at the future. A causal mask blocks every token from looking at anything after it, which keeps next-token training honest.
segments.scene: The real 23×23 attention matrix of layer 2 head 4 on the prompt: lower triangle colored by weight, the upper triangle (future positions) blocked in dark red and outlined.

objects.label: causal mask: positions after the query get weight 0 (score −∞)
last row: what the final " the" attends to

title: The MLP: where tokens think alone
subtitle: Expand, GELU, project back: real neurons in TinyGPT that detect patterns and push predictions

segments.text: Attention lets tokens share information. Then every token goes off alone, through a small network called the MLP. It holds two thirds of each layer's weights.
segments.scene: One transformer layer: an attention box ('tokens share information') above an MLP box ('each token thinks alone'). A bar splits each layer's weights: attention 16,640 vs MLP 33,088 (67%).

objects.label: attention: mixes information between token positions
MLP: processes each token's vector on its own
per layer: attention 16,640 weights, MLP 33,088 weights (66.5%)

segments.text: Inside, it's three steps. Expand the token's 64 numbers into 256 neurons. Pass each one through GELU, which lets positive signals through and squashes negative ones to nearly zero. Then project back down to 64, and add the result to the token's vector.
segments.scene: Network diagram: 64 inputs (blue) fan out to 256 hidden neurons (yellow; drawn 2 per dot) then back to 64 outputs (teal). Inset: the real GELU curve (negative in → ~0, positive in → passes). The output is added back to the token's vector.

objects.label: W_in: 64 × 256 weights (+256 biases) expand the vector
GELU(x) ≈ x for large positive x, ≈ 0 for negative x; GELU(-1) = -0.159, GELU(1) = 0.841
W_out: 256 × 64 weights (+64 biases) project back to 64 numbers

segments.text: Here are the real 256 neuron values in layer 3, for the last word of our story. Most stay quiet. Only 18 percent fire above 0.1.

title: Next token: logits, softmax & temperature
subtitle: How 256 raw scores become one sampled word

segments.text: The model never outputs a word. It outputs 256 numbers. Here's how those turn into one word.
segments.scene: A wall of 256 thin bars — the model's real raw scores for every token in the vocab after the prompt; the tallest (pink) is ' red'.

objects.label: all 256 logits for the prompt (min -5.88, max 10.37)

segments.text: These raw scores are called logits. For our prompt, red scores 10.4, white 7.7, purple 7.5. Two thirds of the vocab sits below zero.
segments.scene: Bar chart of the six highest logits: ' red' 10.37, ' white' 7.68, ' purple' 7.53, ' black' 4.62, ' ava' 3.98, ',' 3.72; the other 250 range from 3.61 down to −5.88.

segments.text: Softmax turns them into probabilities. Raise e to each logit, then divide by the total. Exponentials blow small gaps up into big ones, so red ends up with 87 percent.
segments.scene: The logit bars morph into probability bars: ' red' 87.1%, ' white' 5.9%, ' purple' 5.1%, ' black' 0.28%, ' ava' 0.15%, ',' 0.11%, all 250 others together ~1.4%. Formula: p = exp(logit) / sum of exp over all 256.

objects.label: all 250 other tokens together = 1.42% at T = 1

segments.text: Temperature divides every logit before the softmax. At temperature one, nothing changes.
segments.scene: A big 'T = 1.0' dial appears top right; the bars stay at their T = 1 values.

objects.label: all 250 other tokens together = 1.42% at T = 1

segments.text: Turn it down to 0.3, and the gaps get stretched. Red jumps to 99.98 percent. Basically deterministic.
segments.scene: T slides to 0.3: ' red' grows to 99.98%, every other bar collapses to ~0.

objects.label: all 250 other tokens together = 0.00% at T = 0.3

segments.text: Crank it to 2, and everything flattens. Red drops to 32 percent, and almost half the probability leaks into the long tail of junk.
segments.scene: T slides to 2.0: ' red' falls to 32.4%, ' white' 8.4%, ' purple' 7.8%, and the 250 others together reach 47.1%.

objects.label: all 250 other tokens together = 47.08% at T = 2

segments.text: Top k is the safety net. Keep only the k best tokens, zero out the rest, and renormalize. With k equals 3, the junk is gone, and red is back to 67 percent.

title: Backprop: blame flows backwards
subtitle: The chain rule on a toy graph, then TinyGPT's real gradients for one prediction

segments.text: TinyGPT guessed red at 87 percent: the loss is 0.14. Which of its 170,560 weights should change, and by how much? Backprop answers for all of them, in one sweep backwards.
segments.scene: The end of the probe prompt '… tom has the' → ' red' at 87.1%, loss 0.138; below, a grid of dots standing for the model's 170,560 weights with the question 'which ones are to blame?'.

objects.label: TinyGPT has 170,560 trainable weights (dots are a stand-in)

segments.text: A toy version first. Forward: two times three is six, plus one is seven. That misses the target five by two. Squared, the loss is four.
segments.scene: Toy computational graph (labelled toy): x = 2 and w = 3 feed a × node giving a = 6; a and b = 1 feed a + node giving z = 7; (z − t)² with target t = 5 gives loss L = 4. Forward values in teal.

objects.label: squared error node: L = (z − t)², target t = 5

segments.text: Now backwards. The loss's slope at z is twice the miss: four. A plus node passes blame straight through, so a and b both get four. A times node scales it by the other input: w gets eight, x gets twelve.
segments.scene: Backward pass on the toy graph, gradients in orange flowing right-to-left: ∂L/∂z = 2(z − 5) = 4; the + node copies it: ∂L/∂a = 4, ∂L/∂b = 4; the × node multiplies by the other input: ∂L/∂w = 4 × 2 = 8, ∂L/∂x = 4 × 3 = 12.

objects.label: squared error node: L = (z − t)², target t = 5

segments.text: Brute-force check: nudge w by a hair, and the loss moves eight times as much. Each node just multiplies the blame from above by its own local slope.
segments.scene: Finite-difference check of the toy gradient: (L(w+ε) − L(w−ε))/2ε with ε = 0.0001 gives 8.0000, matching ∂L/∂w = 8. Rule shown on top: blame in = blame from above × local slope.

objects.label: squared error node: L = (z − t)², target t = 5
chain rule: gradient = upstream gradient × local derivative

segments.text: Now the real thing. At TinyGPT's output, each logit's blame is simply its probability, minus one for the right answer. Red: minus 0.13, push up. White and purple: plus 0.06 and 0.05, push down.
segments.scene: Real gradient of the loss w.r.t. TinyGPT's output logits on the probe prompt (target ' red'): ∂loss/∂logit = p − onehot. ' red' -0.129 (teal, push up), ' white' +0.059, ' purple' +0.051, ' black' +0.0028, ' ava' +0.0015 (orange, push down); the other 251 are each between 0 and +0.0010.

objects.label: gradient of cross-entropy w.r.t. logits = softmax probability − one-hot target
the remaining 251 logits each get a small positive gradient (max 0.0010); all 256 sum to -8.3e-17 ≈ 0

segments.text: That blame flows down through all three layers, adding up wherever paths merge. From this single prediction, 167,922 weights get some blame.
segments.scene: Real gradient norms per part of TinyGPT for this one prediction, top (output) to bottom (input): final LayerNorm 0.10, layer 3 MLP 0.84, layer 3 attention 1.06, layer 2 MLP 1.93, layer 2 attention 2.82, layer 1 MLP 3.34, layer 1 attention 5.09, position embedding 2.14, token embedding (tied) 2.84. 167,922 of 170,560 weights have a nonzero gradient.

objects.label: 167,922 of 170,560 weights have nonzero gradient here (unused positions 23–63 get none)

segments.text: Zoom into one real weight. Its gradient is minus 0.07. Negative means: increase me, and the loss drops. A step at learning rate 0.003 adds just 0.0002.
segments.scene: Heat map of the real gradient of layer 3's MLP output matrix (64×256). Highlighted: row 57, column 212, weight 0.0974, gradient -0.0702 (finite-difference check -0.0702). Gradient step at lr 0.003: −lr × grad = +0.00021, new weight 0.0976.

objects.label: weight [57, 212] of layer 3 MLP output: 0.09740, gradient -0.07018

segments.text: But take that raw step on every weight at once, and it overshoots: red falls to 51 percent. TinyGPT's training first shrinks the whole gradient to length one; then the same step lifts red to 87.5.
segments.scene: Two real outcomes of one gradient step at lr 0.003 on all 170,560 weights: raw gradient (length 7.95) → p(red) 87.1% → 50.6% (overshoot); gradient clipped to length 1 like train.py does → 87.1% → 87.5%.

objects.label: gradient clipped to norm 1 (from 7.954), lr 0.003: p(red) 0.8707 → 0.8746

segments.text: Why does backward cost about twice forward? Each matrix multiply going forward needs two going back: one for blame on its inputs, one for blame on its weights. So a training step costs roughly three forward passes, and must keep every activation in memory.
segments.scene: Matrix diagram: forward Y = X·W (one multiply); backward dX = dY·Wᵀ (blame for inputs) and dW = Xᵀ·dY (blame for weights): two multiplies. Tally: forward ≈ 1, backward ≈ 2, training step ≈ 3 units (approximate). Note: activations must be stored for the backward pass.

objects.label: forward: Y = X·W, one matrix multiply per layer weight
backward: dX = dY·Wᵀ passes the gradient to the layer's input
backward: dW = Xᵀ·dY is the gradient for the weights
rule of thumb: backward ≈ 2× forward FLOPs, so a training step ≈ 3× a forward pass (approximate; depends on implementation)
backprop needs the forward activations, so training uses much more memory than inference

segments.text: Forward, backward, nudge. TinyGPT did that three thousand times. Go watch the gradients flow.
segments.scene: Recap loop: forward (get the loss) → backward (share the blame) → nudge every weight, looping back, × 3,000 steps. Final card: 'watch the gradients in the Backprop lab'.

title: Optimizers: learning rate, momentum & Adam
subtitle: Why the learning rate is the knob that matters most, and why AdamW is the default (real sweeps)

segments.text: Same model, same data, same 1,000 steps. The only thing that changed is one number: the learning rate. And it decides everything.
segments.scene: Real validation-loss curves of TinyGPT trained 1000 steps with AdamW at 7 learning rates (1e-4 … 0.1): lr 1e-4 → 1.74, lr 3e-4 → 0.81, lr 1e-3 → 0.66, lr 3e-3 → 0.55, lr 0.01 → 0.55, lr 0.03 → 1.13, lr 0.1 → 3.72.

objects.label: 7 real AdamW runs, 1000 steps each, differing only in learning rate

segments.text: Picture the loss as a landscape and the weights as a ball. The gradient is the slope under the ball. Step downhill by the learning rate times the slope. Repeat.
segments.scene: Toy 1-D loss landscape (illustration) with a yellow ball, an orange tangent showing the slope, and the update rule w ← w − lr × slope; the ball takes 8 steps downhill.

objects.label: gradient descent update: w ← w − lr × slope

segments.text: Too small, and you crawl. Just right, and you settle in a few steps. Too big, and every step overshoots the valley, bouncing higher and higher.
segments.scene: Three toy bowls (illustration): too small (creeps), just right (settles), too big (overshoots, bouncing out of the valley).

objects.label: toy illustration: learning rate too small
toy illustration: learning rate just right
toy illustration: learning rate too big

segments.text: The real runs agree. Learning rate 0.0001 is still crawling at 1.74. 0.003 reaches 0.55. At 0.1, it thrashes around and ends at 3.72.
segments.scene: Real AdamW validation curves: lr 1e-4 (too small) ends at 1.74, lr 3e-3 (best) ends at 0.55, lr 0.1 (too big) ends at 3.72.

objects.label: real AdamW run, lr 1e-4: final val 1.74, best 1.743
real AdamW run, lr 3e-3: final val 0.55, best 0.546
real AdamW run, lr 0.1: final val 3.72, best 3.374

segments.text: Real loss landscapes have long, narrow valleys. Plain gradient descent zigzags across the walls and barely moves along the floor. Momentum keeps a running average of past steps, so the zigzags cancel and it picks up speed.
segments.scene: Toy 2-D elongated valley (illustration, contour ellipses). Top: plain gradient descent zigzags and covers little ground in 30 steps; bottom: momentum (β=0.8) builds speed along the floor.

objects.label: toy: plain gradient descent zigzags across the valley
toy: momentum averages steps and speeds along the floor

segments.text: On the real model, the best plain SGD run ends at 0.74. With momentum, 0.57.
segments.scene: Real runs, best learning rate of each: SGD (lr 1) → 0.74, SGD + momentum 0.9 (lr 0.3) → 0.57.

objects.label: real: best plain SGD (lr 1) final val 0.74

segments.text: Here's the catch. In the real model at step zero, typical gradient sizes differ by 274 times between weight tensors. One learning rate is too big for some and too small for others.
segments.scene: Real per-weight gradient size (RMS of the gradient) for 8 of TinyGPT's tensors at initialisation, log scale: from 7.1e-05 (blocks.0.ln1.weight) to 1.9e-02 (blocks.0.attn_out.bias), a 274× spread.

objects.label: blocks.0.ln1.weight: gradient RMS 7.11e-05 per weight at step 0
blocks.0.attn_qkv.weight: gradient RMS 2.91e-04 per weight at step 0
pos.weight: gradient RMS 6.67e-04 per weight at step 0
blocks.1.mlp_in.weight: gradient RMS 1.30e-03 per weight at step 0
ln_f.weight: gradient RMS 3.14e-03 per weight at step 0
tok.weight: gradient RMS 9.14e-03 per weight at step 0
blocks.1.attn_out.bias: gradient RMS 1.73e-02 per weight at step 0
blocks.0.attn_out.bias: gradient RMS 1.95e-02 per weight at step 0

segments.text: Adam fixes that. It keeps two running averages for every single weight: the gradient, which is momentum, and the gradient squared. Dividing one by the square root of the other gives every weight its own step size.
segments.scene: Adam's update: step = lr × avg(gradient) / √avg(gradient²). Top term = momentum (smoothed direction); bottom = each weight's own typical gradient size, so every weight moves about lr per step.

objects.label: Adam: step = lr × avg(g) / sqrt(avg(g²)) (+ small ε), per weight
Adam normalises step sizes per weight

segments.text: AdamW is Adam plus weight decay applied straight to the weights. In our sweep, 3 of its learning rates landed near the best, across a 10-fold range. Momentum SGD, 2. Plain SGD, none. Tuned momentum gets close on a model this small, but AdamW forgives a rough guess. That's why it's the default for training transformers.
segments.scene: Grid of every real sweep run (learning rate → final val loss). Teal boxes are within 25% of the best (0.68): AdamW 3/7, SGD+momentum 2/4, SGD 0/4.

objects.label: SGD + momentum lr 1: final val NaN (diverged)

segments.text: So: start with AdamW, sweep the learning rate in steps of three, warm up then decay, and if the loss spikes, turn it down.
segments.scene: Recap pills: start with AdamW; sweep the learning rate ×3 at a time; warm up, then decay; loss spikes → lower it.

segments.text: Why? Without the plus, a signal passes through every layer in a chain, and each one rescales it. Shrink a little twenty-four times and it vanishes. Grow a little and it explodes.
segments.scene: Toy arithmetic (illustration): a chain of ×0.6 blocks; 0.6^24 = 4.7e-06 (vanishes), 1.5^24 = 16,834 (explodes).

segments.text: Here's the real thing: a freshly built 24-layer TinyGPT, measuring how much gradient reaches each layer. Without residuals, by the first layer it has shrunk by a factor of 10 to the 17. Those layers can't learn. With residuals, it's nearly flat.
segments.scene: Real measurement, 24-layer TinyGPT at initialisation: RMS of the gradient reaching each layer (log scale). Without residuals (pink) it falls from 4.9e-04 at the top to 2.0e-21 at the input (×10^-17); with residuals (teal) it stays ≈ 5.5e-05–4.3e-05.

objects.label: real: gradient RMS without residuals, 4.92e-04 at the top layer → 1.98e-21 at the embeddings
real: gradient RMS with residuals, 4.33e-05 → 5.51e-05: nearly flat

segments.text: The plus sign builds a highway. The signal travels straight along it, and each block just reads from it and adds a small edit back. On the way back, the gradient rides the same highway, untouched by the plus signs.
segments.scene: Diagram: a yellow 'residual stream' arrow left to right; attention and MLP blocks branch off it and add their output back through '+' nodes; a pink arrow below shows the gradient flowing straight back through every +.

segments.text: Residuals keep the signal alive, but adding edits layer after layer lets its size drift. LayerNorm resets it: subtract the mean, divide by the spread, then let a learned gain and bias pick the scale.

title: Scaling laws: bigger, predictably
subtitle: Seven real TinyGPTs from ~10k to ~1.8M parameters, a fitted power law, and what Kaplan & Chinchilla found

segments.text: Seven TinyGPTs, from 8 thousand to 1.8 million parameters. Same data, same 3.1 million tokens each. Bigger models land lower, with smaller gains at the top.

title: From TinyGPT to ChatGPT
subtitle: Same engine, very different scale: pretraining, instruction tuning, RLHF, chat tokens, KV cache

segments.text: ChatGPT runs the same loop as TinyGPT: read the tokens, score every possible next one, pick, append, repeat. Same building blocks too: embeddings, attention, MLPs.
segments.scene: TinyGPT's loop as boxes: tokens → embed → [attention → MLP] × 3 layers → probabilities → pick one, with an arrow looping back ('append it & repeat'). ChatGPT-style models use the same loop.

objects.label: the generation loop: append the picked token, run again

segments.text: The big difference is scale. GPT-2, in 2019, ranged from 124 million to 1.5 billion parameters. GPT-3, in 2020: 175 billion, 96 layers, vectors 12,288 wide. That's about a million TinyGPTs.
segments.scene: Log-scale bar chart of published parameter counts: TinyGPT 170,560 (3 layers, width 64), GPT-2 small 124M (12 layers, width 768), GPT-2 XL 1.5B (48 layers, width 1,600), GPT-3 175B (96 layers, width 12,288). GPT-3 ≈ 1,026,032 × TinyGPT.

segments.text: Stage one, pretraining: TinyGPT's exact game, on a huge pile of web text. GPT-3 saw about 300 billion tokens; TinyGPT's world is 1.7 million. The result is a base model: an autocomplete, not an assistant. Ask it something, and it may just continue the document.
segments.scene: Log-scale bars of training tokens: TinyGPT's corpus 1,686,858 tokens vs GPT-3 ≈ 300 billion tokens (published). Caption: same game, predict the next token. Illustration: a base model continuing 'Q: What is the capital of France?' with more questions instead of answering.

segments.text: Stage two: supervised fine-tuning. Same loss, now on example conversations written by people: a request, and a good response. The model learns to play the assistant.

segments.text: Stage three, preference tuning. A person picks the better of two answers. A reward model learns those picks, and reinforcement learning nudges the chat model toward high reward, with a penalty for drifting too far. That's RLHF, as in InstructGPT, 2022.

title: The research loop: test your own idea
subtitle: Hypothesis → smallest experiment → baseline → one change → compare → scale. A real TinyGPT experiment

segments.text: Inventing a new model isn't one big idea. It's a loop: a hypothesis, the smallest experiment that could test it, a baseline, one change, an honest comparison, and only then, scale up what wins. Let's run it, for real, on TinyGPT.
segments.scene: The research loop as six pills around a circle: hypothesis → smallest experiment → baseline → change ONE thing → compare across seeds → scale up what wins → back to hypothesis.

objects.label: research loop step 4: change ONE thing
research loop step 5: compare across seeds
research loop step 6: scale up what wins

segments.text: Hypothesis: TinyGPT doesn't need its position embeddings. Attention by itself ignores word order, but the causal mask leaks some: each token sees a different number of tokens before it. So maybe it can work out positions on its own.
segments.scene: TinyGPT's input = token embedding + position embedding, with the position embedding crossed out: 'what if TinyGPT had no position embeddings?'. A 6×6 causal mask: token k sees k tokens, so some order information leaks in.

objects.label: token embedding: one learned vector per token (256 × 64)
position embedding: one learned vector per position (64 × 64 = 4,096 weights)
hypothesis: TinyGPT does not need learned position embeddings
causal mask: each position attends only to itself and earlier positions
the causal mask gives the model an implicit signal about position

segments.text: The smallest test: two short runs of 600 steps, about four minutes each on my CPU. Same code, same data, same batches, same seed. The baseline is unchanged TinyGPT; the only difference is one line.
segments.scene: Experiment setup (real): both runs use 600 steps, batch 64×64, AdamW lr 0.003, cosine schedule, seed 0, identical batches, CPU with 2 threads (235 s and 195 s). Baseline: x = tok(idx) + pos(t). Variant: x = tok(idx).

objects.label: held fixed: 600 steps, batch 64×64, AdamW lr 3e-3 cosine, seed 0, same batches, same code
variant: position embedding removed (166,464 params used)

segments.text: Then compare, on held-out text, measured on the exact same batches. Baseline: 0.65. No positions: 0.68. Removing them hurt, by about 0.03.
segments.scene: Real validation-loss curves from step 200 to 600 (y axis zoomed to 0.62–0.92): baseline (blue) ends at 0.6524, no-positions (pink) ends at 0.6837; gap +0.0313. Evaluated on the same 24 held-out batches (98,304 tokens).

no-positions val loss: 0.896 at step 200 → 0.684 at step 600
final val loss: baseline 0.6524, no positions 0.6837, gap +0.0313

segments.text: But that's one seed per arm. Rerun with a different seed and both numbers move. A real verdict needs three or more seeds each, and a gap that clearly beats the spread between them. So for now, it's a promising hint, not a result.
segments.scene: Number line of val loss at step 600: baseline seed 0 = 0.6524, no positions seed 0 = 0.6837, each with a ±2×SE measurement-noise bar (SE ≈ 0.0035). Only one seed per arm was run; text: a verdict needs 3+ seeds per arm and a gap clearly bigger than the seed-to-seed spread.

objects.label: rule of thumb: several seeds per arm; compare the gap to the seed spread

segments.text: Three classic traps. Different compute: compare against the released model, trained five times longer, and the gap looks 7 times bigger than it is. One seed: luck can fake a win. And leakage: 55 percent of TinyGPT's held-out lines also appear in training, mostly short templated ones. So part of its validation loss measures memory.
segments.scene: Three trap cards. Different compute: comparing the 600-step no-positions run (0.684) to the released 3,000-step model (0.452, same eval batches) suggests a 0.232 gap, 7.4× the real 0.031. One seed: luck can fake a win. Data leakage: 1,642 of 3,001 held-out lines (54.7%) appear verbatim in the training split: all 1,579 short templated lines (Q&A, counting, pets, days, facts) but only 8 of 526 trade stories.

1,642/3,001 validation lines also occur in the training split; trade stories: 8/526

segments.text: So positions win, for now, at this size. Next: more seeds, then longer runs, then a bigger model, checking the gap holds at every step. Your turn: pick a hypothesis.

title: The frontier: a map for model inventors
subtitle: MoE, state-space models, efficient attention, RoPE, retrieval, diffusion LMs, test-time compute, distillation

segments.text: Want to invent a new kind of model? Here's a map of where people are pushing right now. Each idea swaps out one part of the same engine TinyGPT runs on.
segments.scene: A map: TinyGPT's parts in the centre (tokens & positions, attention, MLP, next-token loss, generation loop) with eight research directions around it, grouped into clusters: longer sequences (RoPE, efficient attention, state-space/Mamba), more model per FLOP (mixture of experts, distillation), knowledge outside the weights (retrieval), new ways to generate (diffusion LMs, test-time compute). Dashed lines show which part each idea replaces.

objects.label: Positions & long context (RoPE): rotate each query and key by an angle set by its position, so position enters the score only as the distance between tokens (replaces the position table)
Linear / efficient attention: approximate or restrict attention (kernel tricks, sparse or sliding windows) so cost grows ~linearly (changes attention)
State-space models (Mamba): a recurrence carries a fixed-size state along the sequence; Mamba makes its updates depend on the input (replaces attention)
Mixture of experts: many expert MLPs; a learned router sends each token to just a few of them (replaces the MLP)
Distillation & small models: train a small student to match a big teacher's full probability distribution, not just the right token (changes the training target (loss))
Retrieval-augmented models: look up relevant documents in an external store and put them into the context (adds to the input (what it reads))
Diffusion language models: start from a fully masked sequence and fill in every position over a few refinement steps (replaces the left-to-right generation loop)
Test-time compute & reasoning: spend more computation per question: write out intermediate steps, or sample many answers and check or vote (changes how the generation loop is used)

segments.text: Position schemes like RoPE rotate queries and keys by position, so scores depend on relative distance. Tricks built on it help stretch context, though using very long contexts well remains hard.
segments.scene: Positions & long context (RoPE) (replaces the position table in TinyGPT). Idea: rotate each query and key by an angle set by its position, so position enters the score only as the distance between tokens. Attacks: a learned table like TinyGPT's has exactly 64 slots: position 65 simply doesn't exist. Open: stretching past the training length only partly works; using very long contexts well is still hard. Refs: RoFormer (Su et al. 2021) · Chen et al. 2023 · Lost in the Middle (Liu et al. 2023).

segments.text: Efficient attention keeps attention, but approximates or restricts it, like sliding windows, to dodge the quadratic cost. FlashAttention, by contrast, stays exact and just computes it smarter.

Attacks: the quadratic score grid: every token scored against every earlier token. Open: approximations often cost some quality; FlashAttention instead stays exact and just runs faster. Refs: Katharopoulos et al. 2020 · Longformer (2020) · FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022).

Attacks: attention cost grows with length squared, and the KV cache grows with every token. Open: how much exact detail a fixed-size state can recall; hybrids that keep a few attention layers are a popular compromise. Refs: S4 (Gu et al. 2021) · Mamba (Gu & Dao 2023).
